title: At least two people killed in Japan as typhoon Dujuan triggers heavy rain, landslides
summary:
Storm triggers landslides and travel chaos while cutting off almost ‌50,000 homes from electricity

Typhoon Dujuan has killed at least two people in Japan, while tens of thousands of houses…

blocks.text: Typhoon Dujuan has killed at least two people in Japan, while tens of thousands of houses near Tokyo remained without power after the storm swept through the region, authorities said on Tuesday.
Dujuan – which brought violent winds of 144km/h (89mph) – was moving away from Japan on Tuesday morning, allowing authorities to downgrade most heavy rain and landslide warnings.

But the typhoon had already caused deaths, destruction and widespread chaos, including disruption of some events at the Asian Games and forcing the early closure in Tokyo of the one of the world’s biggest video game trade fairs.

The city of Yokosuka in Kanagawa prefecture, near Tokyo, reported multiple landslides because of the torrential rain. Mud flowing into a home killed a woman in her 60s in Yokosuka, the public ​broadcaster NHK said. Another person died in Chiba.

blocks.caption: Rescue workers search a house hit by a landslide triggered by Typhoon Dujuan in Miura, Japan. Photograph: KYODO/Reuters

blocks.text: Search operations were continuing for four people missing after the landslides, NHK said.
Almost ‌50,000 households ​were still ​without electricity in Chibam near Tokyo on Tuesday morning, officials said.
The storm forced Japan Airlines to cancel 135 flights and All Nippon Airways to scrap 140.
More than 1.6 million residents in and around Tokyo were urged to evacuate on Monday, according to the Fire and Disaster Management Agency. The evacuations were not mandatory.

blocks.caption: A boy cycles through a flooded street as Typhoon Dujuan brings heavy rain, in Ichikawa, in Chiba prefecture. Photograph: KYODO/Reuters

blocks.text: Although Dujuan weakened as it moved north-east, it dumped record rainfall in parts of the Tokyo area.
Oshima, an island about 120km south of central Tokyo, was drenched with 832mm of rain over 48 hours, more than double its average rainfall for the whole of September, NHK reported.
Rainfall in Tokyo’s Edogawa ward reached a record 282.5mm over 24 hours.

Japan often sees strong typhoons in the late summer and early autumn. But scientists say human-driven climate change is intensifying the risk posed by heavy rains because a warmer atmosphere holds more water.

Typhoon Dujuan is the latest extreme weather event in a ⁠year of unusually intense rain, floods and tropical ​cyclones that have hit ‌regions across ‌the globe, from east Asia to North America ‌and Europe.
